deep.reconstruction:
The page holds no derivation. It is a single prose memorandum, and its handwriting looks more like G. H. Hardy's (or another editor's) than Ramanujan's. It reads: 'Idea. You can replace the Bessel fns of the V. identity by circular functions, at the price of complicating the "sum". Interesting idea, but prob[abl]y of no value for the study of the divisor problem.'

Interpretation (mine). 'V. identity' is almost certainly Voronoi's identity (Voronoi 1904) for the Dirichlet divisor problem. In modern notation, with D(x) = sum'_{n<=x} d(n) (the last term halved if x is an integer):

D(x) = x log x + (2*gamma - 1) x + 1/4 - sqrt(x) * sum_{n>=1} d(n)/sqrt(n) * [ Y_1(4 pi sqrt(n x)) + (2/pi) K_1(4 pi sqrt(n x)) ].

The remark says one can trade the Bessel kernels Y_1 and K_1 for trigonometric kernels, at the cost of a more complicated arithmetic sum. Two standard ways of doing this exist.

(a) Go back to Dirichlet's hyperbola method. This gives D(x) = 2 sum_{n<=sqrt x} floor(x/n) - floor(sqrt x)^2. Writing floor(t) = t - 1/2 - psi(t) and expanding psi(t) = -sum_{m>=1} sin(2 pi m t)/(pi m) yields Delta(x) = -2 sum_{n<=sqrt x} psi(x/n) + O(1). This is a finite double sum of sines of 2 pi m x/n: circular functions, but a 'complicated sum'.

(b) Use the asymptotic form of the kernels: Y_1(z) ~ sqrt(2/(pi z)) sin(z - 3 pi/4), while K_1 is exponentially small. This gives Hardy's truncated form Delta(x) ≈ x^{1/4}/(pi sqrt 2) * sum_{n<=N} d(n) n^{-3/4} cos(4 pi sqrt(n x) - pi/4) + error.

The writer judges such reformulations unlikely to help with the order of Delta(x). This is consistent with Hardy's own work on the divisor problem from 1915–1916.

There is no evident link to the preceding page (U_n, V_n as polynomials in P, Q, R) or the following page (pi series, q-products). The folio appears to be a stray editorial or Hardy note filed among Ramanujan's papers. The previous page carries the annotation 'dont know just what this belongs to'.

results.what: Remark that the Bessel-function kernels in Voronoi's formula for the divisor problem can be replaced by trigonometric functions at the cost of a more complicated arithmetic sum; judged probably useless for the divisor problem.
results.modern_name: Voronoi summation formula for d(n); hyperbola-method / Fourier (sawtooth) expansion of Delta(x); Hardy's truncated Voronoi series
results.usually_credited_to: G. Voronoi (1904) for the Bessel identity; Dirichlet (1849) for the hyperbola method; G. H. Hardy (1915–16) and Hardy–Landau for trigonometric and truncated forms
